latvian gambit.intro: We're playing the white side of the Latvian Gambit, a sharp and unsound opening where Black pushes the f-pawn early, weakening their kingside. Our plan is to open the center and exploit the exposed king with simple, forceful moves.
latvian gambit.shortIntro: White punishes Black's early f5 with central play and direct threats.
latvian gambit.outro: By opening the center and targeting the weak f7 square, we've built a winning attack. Simple development and concrete tactics are all it takes to refute the Latvian Gambit.

ideas.text: e4 opens the game, claiming central space and freeing your bishop and queen. It's the standard first move, setting the stage for active play.
e5 is Black's natural reply, mirroring your central pawn. The game is now in classic open-game territory.
Nf3 develops the knight to its best square, attacking e5 and preparing to castle. This is the most common and principled move.
f5 is the Latvian Gambit, a dubious move that weakens Black's kingside and opens diagonals. Black hopes to surprise you, but we'll punish it by opening the center with d4.
Bc4 develops the bishop to a powerful diagonal, eyeing f7—the weakest square in Black's camp. This move increases pressure and threatens immediate checkmate if Black isn't careful.
fxe4 captures your e4 pawn, but Black's king is now even more exposed. Instead of recapturing automatically, we look for a more forceful continuation.
Nxe5 sacrifices the knight temporarily, but it opens the e5 square for your queen. This is a classic idea: trade on e5 to deliver a devastating check on h5.
Qg5 is Black's attempt to defend f7 and counterattack, but it leaves the queen misplaced. We now have a powerful follow-up: Nf7 forks the queen and rook.
Nf7 forks Black's queen and rook, winning material. This knight jump is the direct punishment for Black's careless play—the queen must move, and we'll capture the rook.

Qxg2 — Black ignores the fork, snapping off a pawn and attacking the rook on h1. It looks scary, but the queen has wandered far from her own king, and your fork on f7 still wins the exchange. Defend calmly and the counterplay evaporates.
ideas.shortText: Qxg2 ignores the fork and attacks the rook on h1.

ideas.text: Rf1 is a quiet but essential move. It gets the rook off the back rank and prepares to join the attack, while also defending the f2 pawn. Black's king is still exposed, and we want to bring all our pieces into the game.
ideas.shortText: Rf1 brings the rook into play.

ideas.text: d5 is a desperate attempt by Black to block the diagonal and gain space. But it doesn't solve the king's safety issues. We can simply continue our development, as Black's position remains full of holes.
Nxh8 collects the cornered rook. The knight may take a few moves to find its way out of h8, but the material is decisive and Black's king remains the one in real danger.
ideas.shortText: Nxh8 collects the rook in the corner.

ideas.text: Nf6 is a final blunder, but the game is already lost. Black's knight moves to f6, but it doesn't defend anything crucial. We can now finish with a simple tactic, like Qe2+ followed by Rd1, winning the queen.
